posts.caption: My mare found the mirror in our tack room in August and hasn't walked past it since. Every morning she stops, turns her good side, and holds still until I say her name twice. The farrier once waited twenty minutes while she checked her left profile. I stopped fighting it around Labor Day. Last week I caught myself fixing my own hair in the same mirror, so I understand now. She watched me do it from the doorway like I was late to a meeting I'd called.
posts.first: She has never once walked past a reflection on purpose. Puddles, the trough, the truck's side mirror, the shiny bucket. I've bought her a brush for every one of her complaints and she still prefers the bucket. I've learned to build in an extra five minutes.

posts.caption: Our farrier is a patient man with forty years of knees and a truck that smells like hoof dressing. He arrives at 7:40 with a thermos and a list. Red greets him at the stall door like a customer who has a complaint. He asks nicely, he asks twice, and he has learned to drink his coffee in between. I've offered to hold her and she's offered me a look. By nine he's done and she's standing like a statue, as if none of it was her idea.
posts.first: He told me once that the worst horses he's trimmed taught him the most, and that Red is in the top three. I took it as a compliment on my behalf. He didn't correct me. He did raise his price a dollar that month.

posts.quote: A hay delivery is mostly a long conversation with a man who has strong opinions about next year's rain.
posts.first: Our hay guy has delivered to this barn for eleven years and has never once admitted it was a good growing season. He pulls in around four, backs the truck up to the loft, and we stand there talking about the sky until the bales are stacked. I've never known whether to tip him or just agree.

posts.caption: The first hard freeze always arrives with a text from my neighbor, who has a thermometer on every fence post. By 5:45 I'm in my husband's coat and the good socks, thawing the trough with a kettle. The mare watches from her stall like a customer who's been kept waiting. I break the ice, carry the warm buckets, and check her blanket twice. She accepts all of it without comment. Then she lets out a long breath and leans her head against my shoulder for exactly three seconds.
posts.first: We don't talk about the three seconds. She lets me have them if nobody is watching, and the barn cat is the only one who is. I stood there until my feet went numb last winter. I'd do it again, thermometer permitting.

posts.caption: My gelding turned twenty-nine this fall and has never been more punctual. Supper is at four and he's at the gate by 3:40, facing the feed room like a man waiting on a bus. Everything else is negotiable. He'll stand for the farrier, tolerate the vet, and ignore the trailer entirely. I stopped scheduling around his knees years ago and started scheduling around his stomach. It's the only calendar he's ever agreed to. He's early every single day.
posts.first: He came to me at nineteen with a bad hock and a worse attitude. Ten years later the hock is fine and the attitude has softened into something I'd call dignity. He still pins his ears at the wheelbarrow. Some principles should be kept.

posts.caption: Our pony has a system. After the last carrot of the evening he goes to the paddock gate and stands there like a painting. He tilts his head, lifts one ear, and lets the forelock fall just so. I've held out through three snowstorms and a broken water heater. Last night he added a small sigh and I felt it in my knees. I gave him half a carrot. He accepted it the way a banker accepts a deposit.
posts.first: He has never once gone for the treats directly. He waits, he performs, and he lets me believe it was my idea. My husband says I've been out-negotiated by a creature that stands thirty-six inches tall. I told him the pony has a stronger case.
